claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is primarily a homogeneous, single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Mechanical alloying followed by hot isostatic pressing can introduce a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion into HfNbTaTiZr.
Hot isostatic pressing at 1200–1600°C is an appropriate consolidation window for the proposed ODS alloy.
The processing route will produce uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles embedded in the BCC matrix.
The embedded Y2O3 nanoparticles will be thermodynamically stable.
Nanoscale Y2O3 particles obstruct dislocation motion in the HfNbTaTiZr matrix.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by Y2O3 particles increases alloy strength.
Nanoscale Y2O3 particles hinder the migration and clustering of irradiation-induced defects.
The thermal and irradiation stability of Y2O3 particles helps prevent phase degradation.
Relative to HfNbTaTiZr without Y2O3, the ODS alloy will have higher yield strength at 800–1000°C.
Relative to HfNbTaTiZr without Y2O3, the ODS alloy will have a lower creep rate at 800–1000°C.
The ODS alloy will maintain phase stability during elevated-temperature exposure and ion irradiation to 1–5 dpa.
The ODS alloy will exhibit limited irradiation-induced embrittlement relative to the unmodified alloy.
The proposed benefits depend critically on retaining a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion.
Agglomeration or coarsening of Y2O3 during high-temperature exposure could reduce the strengthening and creep-resistance benefits.
Similar ODS approaches in steels and Ni-based superalloys provide supportive prior evidence.
Direct evidence for ODS strengthening in refractory high-entropy alloys is limited.
